explain.say: In 1529 an Ottoman army camped outside Vienna, in the heart of Europe. Its sultan, Suleiman, ruled from Hungary to Baghdad, from Algeria to Mecca. Europeans called him the Magnificent; his own people called him Kanuni, the lawgiver. Look at the timeline of the empire at its height.

explain.say: See the map. In 1517 Suleiman's father, Selim, took Egypt and became protector of Mecca and Medina, a huge source of prestige. Suleiman added Hungary after Mohács in 1526 and Baghdad in 1534. Why would guarding the holy cities matter to a Muslim ruler's authority?

Now the network. Look at the Balkan villages. Through the devshirme, officials took Christian boys, converted them to Islam and trained them as Janissary soldiers or palace officials. It was a form of enslavement, yet some rose to grand vizier, the top minister. How can a system be both forced and a path to power?

The empire ruled many faiths. Orthodox Christians, Armenians and Jews kept their own religious leaders and courts, and in 1492 Sultan Bayezid II welcomed Jews expelled from Spain. The architect Sinan built hundreds of buildings, like the Süleymaniye mosque, finished in 1557. What does welcoming refugees suggest about Ottoman priorities?

explain.say: Did it decline after Suleiman died in 1566? See the debate. Older Western writers said yes; historians like Cemal Kafadar and Baki Tezcan describe transformation, and the empire lasted until 1922. Excellent work. Exam tip: never write decline without saying who says so and why.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Most historians now reject simple decline.

faq.a: Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, called Kanuni, the lawgiver, by his subjects. He conquered Hungary and Baghdad, besieged Vienna in 1529, issued law codes and sponsored the architect Sinan.
asks: Why was Suleiman called the lawgiver?

faq.a: A levy of Christian boys, mostly from the Balkans, who were taken from their families, converted to Islam and trained for the Janissary corps or palace service. It was a form of slavery, but its members could rise to the highest offices.

faq.q: How did the Ottoman Empire rule so many peoples?
faq.a: Through a strong central army and administration, local elites, tax-farming, and religious communities that ran their own affairs under their leaders, while recognising the sultan's authority. Historians note the formal millet system was mostly a later, nineteenth-century development.

faq.q: Why did the Ottomans welcome Jews from Spain?
faq.a: After Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, Sultan Bayezid II invited them to settle in Ottoman lands, where many became merchants, doctors and printers in cities like Istanbul and Salonica.
asks: What happened after 1492 to Sephardic Jews?

faq.q: Did the Ottoman Empire decline after Suleiman?
faq.a: The old decline thesis is now widely rejected. Historians such as Cemal Kafadar and Baki Tezcan show the empire adapting its army, finances and politics, and it survived until 1922, though it lost wars and territory after 1683.
asks: What is the Ottoman decline thesis?

facts: Suleiman the Magnificent reigned from 1520 to 1566.
The Ottomans defeated Hungary at Mohács in 1526.
The Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul, designed by Sinan, was completed in 1557.

quiz.say: What was Suleiman's title among his own people?
quiz.why: Kanuni means lawgiver, for his law codes.

wrong.1: The Conqueror, Fatih, was Mehmed II, who took Constantinople.
wrong.2: The Magnificent was the European name for him.

quiz.say: Which statement best fits recent research on the Ottomans after 1566?
quiz.why: Historians like Tezcan describe a 'second empire' adapting to new conditions.

wrong.2: Armies, finance and politics all changed.
